Simply stay lying here and breathe. If you fall asleep, that's exactly right. The day is over. You did your best. You're allowed to rest now. Good night.

map.[0:00 · ARRIVING]\n\nGood morning, wild:
[0:00 · ARRIVING]

Good morning, wild hearts. Good morning.

Let me say hello to everyone who woke up early for this. {names}. I'm so happy you're here.

Maybe you're still in your pyjamas. Maybe you have your first coffee or tea in your hands. Maybe the house is still quiet, or maybe it's already loud and you just snuck away for a few minutes. Every version of you is welcome this morning.

This is {title}. Before the day starts pulling at you, we're taking fifteen minutes that are only yours. Camera on or off, sitting or lying down, it's all fine.

[pause]

[1:30 · SETTING UP]

Let's make your space a little cosy first.

If you can, sit somewhere you can lean back. Put your drink down next to you. Wrap a blanket around your shoulders if you like.

And just notice: how did you wake up this morning? Rested? Tired? Already with a list in your head?

You don't need to change anything. Just notice it, and say good morning to yourself.

[pause]

[2:30 · WHY WE BREATHE IN THE MORNING]

This morning we're going to do a short breathwork practice together. Nothing wild, nothing intense. Just your breath, a little slower and a little deeper than usual.

The way we breathe tells our nervous system how safe we are. When we start the day already rushing, our breath gets short and shallow, high up in the chest. And our body thinks: something is wrong, hurry.

So we're going to tell it something different this morning.

One small note before we start: if you feel dizzy at any point, just go back to your normal breath. Your body always knows best. And if you're pregnant, keep everything soft and gentle, with no breath holds.

[3:30 · BREATHWORK: ARRIVING BREATH]

Place one hand on your belly and one hand on your chest.

Breathe in through your nose, and let the hand on your belly rise first.

Breathe out through your nose, slowly, and feel the belly sink.

[breathe together, five slow breaths, about one minute]

Good. Notice how the hand on your belly moves more than the one on your chest. That's the breath that calms you.

[5:00 · BREATHWORK: BOX BREATHING]

Now we'll add a gentle rhythm. It's called box breathing, and it's one I come back to on the busy mornings at home.

Breathe in for four … two, three, four.

Hold gently for four … two, three, four.

Breathe out for four … two, three, four.

And hold empty for four … two, three, four.

[guide four rounds, about two minutes, counting slowly]

And let the rhythm go. Breathe naturally.

[8:00 · A MORNING STORY]

I want to tell you why I love doing this in the morning.

In our house, mornings can be a lot. Four children, breakfasts, school bags, someone who can't find a shoe, someone who doesn't want to get dressed. And I think so many of us know this: going straight from bed into all of that, and feeling behind before the day has even started.

[your detail: what a real morning in your house looks like, one small moment]

What helps me on the hard days is not a perfect routine. It's the things I learned and teach: slowing my breath, a little gentle movement, a small ritual just for me. A few breaths before I open the door to the day.

The day is still full. But I move through it differently. A little more me, a little less rushing.

[10:00 · YOUR INTENTION]

Before we close, I'd love you to choose one word for today. One word for how you want to move through this day.

Calm. Gentle. Brave. Present. Soft. Strong.

If you like, write your word in the chat, so we can carry each other's words today.

[wait, and read some words out loud with their names]

What beautiful words. Let's keep them with us.

[11:30 · A QUESTION FROM THE CIRCLE]

[If there is a question in the chat or in your questions panel, answer it here. If not, use this one:]

A question I often get is: "What if I don't have fifteen minutes in the morning?"

Then take one minute. Four rounds of box breathing take about one minute. That's enough to tell your body: I'm here, I'm safe, I can do this day. Small and often is so much more powerful than perfect and rare.

[12:30 · AN INVITATION]

If this morning felt good, come back next time. We'll breathe together again.

And if you want a little support for every day, my Reset Routine for Tired Days is free on moveciamovement.com, and my Mindful Movement Method opens on the 1st of December, with short morning sessions just like this one, whenever you have time. You can already book your place.

[If you show an offer this morning: show it now, and say:] I've put something on your screen for you. Have a look whenever it suits you.

[13:30 · CLOSING]

Let's take one last box breath together. In for four … hold … out for four … hold … and let it go.

Put your hand on your heart and say your word to yourself, silently.

Thank you for starting your day with us.

Go gently into your morning, wild hearts. Have a beautiful day.

[0:00 · ARRIVING]

Good morning, wild hearts. Welcome, welcome.

Let me say good morning to each of you. {names}. Thank you for giving this morning to yourself.

Some of you might have woken up before everyone else at home, just for this. Some of you might have children running around in the background. Some of you might still be in bed. All of it is welcome here.

This is {title}. For the next thirty minutes we're going to breathe, move a little, and set an intention for the day. You don't need any experience. You just need to be here. Camera on or off, completely up to you.

[pause]

[2:00 · SETTING UP]

Let's make your space cosy.

Find a seat where your back can be long, on a chair, on the sofa, or on the floor with a cushion under you. Have something to drink next to you, and if you like, a pen and a piece of paper for later.

Wrap a blanket around you if it's cold where you are. Here in the mountains, the mornings are already really chilly.

[pause]

And now just notice how you arrived this morning. Your body. Your mood. Your thoughts. No judgement. Just a quiet good morning to yourself.

[4:00 · A FEW WORDS BEFORE WE START]

I want to say something about breathwork before we begin.

Over the years I've done 1,150 hours of training. Yoga, bodyweight training, rehab, nervous system regulation, Yoga Nidra. And still, the most important things I learned didn't come from any course. They came from my own hardest days. The days when I was tired in a way sleep doesn't fix, with four children and a full life around me.

On those days, my breath was always the first thing I could change. Before my thoughts, before my mood, before anything else.

So this morning we'll start there.

A small note for safety: we'll keep everything gentle. If you feel dizzy at any point, just go back to your normal breath. If you're pregnant, skip any holding of the breath and keep everything soft.

[6:00 · PRACTICE 1: CALM BREATHING]

Close your eyes or let your gaze go soft.

Place one hand on your belly.

We're going to breathe in a slow, even rhythm. In for five, and out for five. This rhythm is one of the most calming ways to breathe, for your heart and for your whole nervous system.

Breathe in … two, three, four, five.

Breathe out … two, three, four, five.

[guide for about three minutes, counting softly at first, then letting them continue in silence]

You can keep counting on your own now. In for five … out for five.

[let them breathe in silence for about one minute]

And let the counting go. Just breathe.

[10:00 · PRACTICE 2: HUMMING BREATH]

Now something a little playful. A humming breath.

Breathe in through your nose. And as you breathe out, keep your lips closed and hum. Like a bee. Mmmmm.

[hum together]

Feel the vibration in your face, your throat, your chest. Humming is one of the kindest things you can do for your nervous system. It's like a little massage from the inside.

Again. Breathe in … and hum.

[five more rounds together]

And rest. Notice how your face feels now. Maybe a little tingly. Maybe softer.

[12:30 · PRACTICE 3: GENTLE MOVEMENT]

Let's wake up the body a little.

Sit tall. Put your hands on your knees.

As you breathe in, open your chest forward and lift your gaze a little.

As you breathe out, round your back and let your chin come towards your chest.

[guide five slow rounds]

Now lift your right arm up and lean gently to the left. Feel the whole side of your body lengthen. Breathe into your ribs.

[hold three breaths]

And back to the middle. Now the left arm up, and lean gently to the right.

[hold three breaths]

And back to the middle. Roll your shoulders a few times, whichever direction feels good.

And let your hands rest.

[16:00 · PRACTICE 4: ALTERNATE NOSTRIL BREATHING]

The last breathing practice brings balance. It's called alternate nostril breathing.

Bring your right hand to your face. Rest your thumb next to your right nostril and your ring finger next to your left nostril.

Close the right side gently with your thumb, and breathe in through the left.

Close the left side with your ring finger, open the right, and breathe out through the right.

Breathe in through the right.

Close the right, open the left, and breathe out through the left.

That's one round. Let's do it together, slowly.

[guide about two minutes; if it feels too complicated for someone, invite them to simply keep breathing in for five, out for five]

And let your hand rest. Breathe normally through both sides.

[pause]

[19:30 · YOUR INTENTION FOR TODAY]

Now take your pen and paper, or just your thoughts.

I'd like you to answer one question for yourself: how do I want to feel at the end of this day?

Not what do I want to get done. How do I want to feel.

Write down one sentence. Or just one word.

[give them about one minute in silence]

And if you'd like, write your word in the chat, so we can carry each other's intentions today.

[wait, and read some words out loud with their names]

[react warmly, for example:] Look at these words. What a beautiful way to start a day.

[22:30 · A QUESTION FROM THE CIRCLE]

[If there is a question in the chat or in your questions panel, answer it here. If not, use this one:]

A question I often get is: "How do I keep this up on normal mornings, when there's no Gathering?"

Start tiny. Choose one practice from this morning, just one. Maybe the humming breath while the kettle boils. Maybe five breaths of in for five, out for five before you get out of bed. One minute a day that you really do is worth so much more than thirty minutes you only plan to do.

[24:30 · A STORY TO TAKE WITH YOU]

I want to share one more thing with you.

When I started my very first personal training sessions, I thought my job was to get women moving. But almost every woman told me sooner or later how exhausted she was. And so often I heard: "I had zero motivation to get up today, but I knew you were coming."

That sentence stayed with me. Because sometimes we don't need more discipline. We need someone who waits for us. A circle that notices when we're there.

That's what I want these mornings to be for you. A place where someone is waiting for you. Where you're expected, and welcome, exactly as you are.

[26:30 · AN INVITATION]

If you'd like to keep coming back to mornings like this, join the next Gathering. They're free, and you'll always find the date on moveciamovement.com.

And if you want this as part of your life, with breathwork, short movement sessions and a new programme every month, my Mindful Movement Method opens on the 1st of December, and you can already book your place.

[If you show an offer this morning: show it now, and say:] I've put something on your screen for you now. Take a look in your own time.

[28:00 · CLOSING]

Let's close with three breaths together. In for five … out for five.

[Talking head · straight to camera · approx. 5 min. · speak calmly and slowly]

Hi there. It's so lovely to have you here.

[take a breath, smile]

Before we do anything else, I'd like you to take a moment to really arrive. Maybe you're sitting on the sofa right now, maybe you're standing in the kitchen while the dishwasher is still running or a child is calling for you. Wherever you are, let your shoulders sink a little and notice that today you decided to do something for yourself. That's already a big step.

I'm Vivien, and I'd like to tell you why this place exists. I have four children and a house full of life, and for a long time I felt that I was there for everyone except myself. There were evenings when I fell into bed exhausted and wondered when I had last truly felt at home in my own body.

[your detail: a moment when you felt this yourself]

I found my way back through movement, the quiet kind of movement where you don't have to prove anything. A few calm minutes on the mat and one deep breath with my hand on my belly were enough to make a little room inside me again. Since 2021 I've had the privilege of walking this path with other women, and almost every one of them has told me about exactly this tiredness at some point. I built the Method for them, and for you.

You begin with Arrive, the first part of the Method. These three videos are fully yours from today: this one, your first gentle flow and a small breathing practice you can come back to whenever everything feels like too much.

After that your first month opens, and every month carries its own theme. Sometimes my voice guides you through a flow and I tell you how to find your way into a movement and what you might feel there. Sometimes you move to a calm timer and your own favourite music. And sometimes we simply sit together like we do now, and I share a thought, a breathing practice or a meditation with you.

I decided on purpose that the next video only opens once you've done the previous one all the way to the end. I know myself well enough: when I have everything in front of me at once, I click around, can't find a beginning and in the end don't stay with anything. Here we take it step by step instead, about three times a week. And if you miss a whole week, your video waits patiently for you, and there's nothing you need to catch up on.

In your space you'll also find your journal. Whatever you write there belongs only to you. Not even I can read it. With every month you'll also receive a workbook with small rituals that fit easily into a busy everyday life.

[pause]

There's one more thing I wish for you: be gentle with yourself. Here you don't have to perform or compare yourself with anyone. If you're pregnant or have just had a baby, please talk to your midwife or doctor first and always choose the easier variation as soon as something doesn't feel right.

If you like, let's roll out the mat together now. Your first flow is already waiting for you, and it's gentle enough to suit you no matter how long it's been since you last moved. I'm so happy you're here. Movement begins with you.

map.Bend your knees as if you were sitting d: Bend your knees as if you were sitting down on a chair and lift your arms forward and up. Your weight is in your heels. It's fine if your thighs start to get warm now, just keep breathing calmly. To come out, straighten your legs and lower your arms.
map.Today is a tired day, and that is comple: Today is one of those tired days, and that is completely all right. Lie down on your back, place your feet on the floor, and pull a blanket over you if you like. Today we'll do almost everything lying down. First let your attention travel to your feet and feel where they touch the floor. Then to your legs, to your pelvis and to your belly, rising and falling with every breath. Feel your shoulders, your neck and your face. You don't have to change anything, you're only noticing how you are today. That is exactly what this first week of Unfold is about, an honest look.
map.Come through your hands into Downward-Fa: Bring your hands to the floor and come into Downward-Facing Dog. Press your hands into the floor and your hips up, and make your back long, even if that means keeping your knees bent.
map.Come to standing and shake yourself out,: Come to standing and shake yourself out, your hands, your arms, your legs, your whole body. Today is one of those tired days, and maybe your head is full of thoughts about your idea. Let's make today feel light.
map.Come to standing and let your gaze wande: Come to standing and let your gaze wander slowly through the room. This week Unfold is about courage and visibility, about letting yourself be seen for who you are and what you're planning. Becoming visible begins in the body, by taking up space. So today, we take up all the room we want.
map.Stretch out long. We'll travel through t: Stretch out long. We'll travel through the body now, and every part gets a thank you. Thank you, dear feet, for carrying me every day. Thank you, dear legs, for every step. Thank you, dear pelvis and dear belly, for everything you have held. Thank you, dear back, for carrying so much. Thank you, dear hands, for everything you do and for every touch. Thank you, dear heart, for beating without ever stopping. Thank you, dear face, for laughing and for crying.
map.Stay here and feel how your body feels a: Stay where you are and notice how your body feels after all this thanks. Maybe a little warmer, maybe a little more loved. Stay here as long as you like.
Streck dich lang aus und lass alles los. Du hast dich entfaltet, ganz im Sinne von Unfold. Du bist nicht fertig, denn niemand ist je fertig, aber du bist weiter aufgegangen, Woche für Woche, wie eine Blüte, die sich langsam öffnet. Was nimmst du mit? Was ist anders als vor dreizehn Wochen? Bleib hier, so lange du magst, und dann geh weiter, in deinem Tempo.
map.Stand with your feet hip-width apart and: Stand with your feet hip-width apart and take a big step back with your left foot. Turn your back foot so it sits almost parallel to the short edge of the mat while your right foot points forward. Bend your right knee until it's roughly over your ankle, and make sure it tracks towards your little toe without collapsing inwards. Lift your arms out to the sides at shoulder height, right arm reaching forward, left arm reaching back, and let your gaze travel over your right fingertips. [breathe calmly] Warrior II is a pose full of quiet strength. I like to imagine that it protects my boundaries whenever lots of demands and commitments are pulling at me. Stay for a few breaths, then straighten your front leg and change sides, with your left foot in front and your right foot behind. To finish, straighten your front leg, turn your feet parallel and bring them hip-width apart.

Let your feet fall loosely to the sides and rest your arms a little away from your body with the palms facing up. If your lower back feels tight, slide a cushion under your knees, and feel free to cover yourself with a blanket. Close your eyes. There is nothing left to get done now. Your breath flows by itself and your body is allowed to grow heavy. [Pause] This month we practise rest just as much as strength, and today you took the very first step. That is more than enough. [Pause] When you're ready, slowly move your fingers and toes, have a good stretch and roll onto your right side. Then press yourself gently up to sitting with your hands. Take a little piece of this calm with you into your day. I'm looking forward to practising with you again next time.
map.The day is over. Lie down comfortably, c:
The day is over. Lie down comfortably, pull a blanket over you and dim the lights. You don't have to do anything else now. This meditation is an invitation to put the day down and soften.

Breathe in through your nose for four, and out through your mouth, long and slow, for six. With every breath out you sink a little deeper into whatever you are lying on.

[kurze Pause, lächeln]

Wenn deine Wirbelsäule beweglich ist, fällt es dir auch leichter, dich aufzurichten und für dich einzustehen.

[Talking head · straight to camera · approx. 8 min.]

Hi, it's lovely to see you again. You've finished your first session, and now I'd like to take a little more time to explain what is actually happening in your body during pregnancy. In the live session there's often not much room for that, and I've seen again and again that women trust their bodies so much more once they understand why everything is changing.

[short pause]

Let's start with a hormone you may have heard of already, relaxin. Your body produces it from the very first weeks of pregnancy, and together with other hormones it makes your ligaments and connective tissue more pliable. There's a good reason for this, because your pelvis needs to be able to widen a little during birth. The flip side is that your joints have a bit less stability than usual right now. You might already notice it when your pelvis feels different as you walk, or when you suddenly sink much deeper into a stretch than you used to. That's exactly where I'd like you to stay careful, because during pregnancy more flexibility doesn't automatically mean it's good for your body. So we move slowly and with control, and in every stretch we stop just short of our limit.

The second thing that changes is your centre of gravity. Month by month your belly grows forward, and your body tries to balance that out all by itself. Many women unconsciously push their pelvis forward or arch their lower back, the shoulders drift backwards and the head pokes forward a little. That's a completely natural reaction, but over time the load ends up in your lower back, and that's where a lot of pregnant women really feel it in the evening. This is why we practised standing alignment. If you come back to it often, while brushing your teeth, waiting at the checkout or cooking dinner, it slowly becomes second nature, and your back gets a little relief every single day.

[your detail: how you felt your back in your own pregnancies]

You may also have noticed that some tops or bras feel tight around your ribs. That's because your lower ribs widen sideways during pregnancy, so your baby has room and your lungs still get enough space. Later on, your growing uterus presses up against your diaphragm, and some women feel as if they can't quite take a full breath anymore. It's uncomfortable, but in the vast majority of cases it's harmless. If you suddenly feel very short of breath, have chest pain or simply sense that something isn't right, please call your doctor or your midwife.

And that brings us to the topic closest to my heart in this first session, the way your breath, your belly and your pelvic floor work together. Imagine your torso as a cylinder. At the top is your diaphragm, the big breathing muscle beneath your ribs, and at the bottom is your pelvic floor. Your deep abdominal muscles wrap around your middle like a wide belt, and at the back small muscles along your spine support the whole structure. When you breathe in, the diaphragm moves down, your ribs expand and your pelvic floor softens slightly downwards. When you breathe out, the diaphragm rises again and your pelvic floor lifts a little along with it, quite naturally. This happens with every single breath, many thousands of times a day, without you having to think about it.

That's why the 360° breathing we practised today is so valuable. When you breathe into your sides, into your back and gently into your belly, this team works the way it's meant to. Many of us breathe quite shallowly and high up in the chest during the day, especially when we're stressed. Then the pelvic floor hardly moves at all, and tension tends to collect in the neck or the jaw. And this breath will carry you beyond the birth as well, because it's the foundation for your core and pelvic floor recovery afterwards.

[pause]

One worry I hear a lot at this stage is whether movement could harm the baby. I understand that so well, I had those thoughts myself. For a healthy pregnancy, though, regular gentle movement is good for you and your baby, and current guidelines actively encourage pregnant women to stay active. What matters is that your doctor or midwife is happy with it and that you listen to your body's signals. If you have any bleeding, leak amniotic fluid, feel regular contractions before 37 weeks or get dizzy, stop straight away and get in touch with them.

In the movement video for this session I'll take you through all the exercises again at a calm pace, from Cat-Cow and seated pelvic circles to the seated side bend and standing alignment. You can come back to it as often as you like, including on the days we don't see each other. In your workbook you'll find the key points from this session and space for your own notes, for example where you can already feel your breath clearly and where it still feels unfamiliar.

Your little task for the next few days is very simple. Three times a day, take five breaths of 360° breathing, perhaps in the morning while you're still in bed, once around lunchtime and once in the evening before you fall asleep. Each time it takes barely a minute, and yet you'll notice how your sense of your own body slowly begins to shift.

[pause, smile]

I'm already looking forward to our next session. If you like, start the movement video now and breathe a few rounds with me.

[Talking head · straight to camera · approx. 8 min.]

Hi, here you are again. In our session we turned our attention to your pelvic floor for the first time, and because it's something we women talk about far too rarely, I'd like to go into it a little more deeply here.

[short pause]

Your pelvic floor isn't a single sheet of muscle. It's made up of several layers of muscle and connective tissue that stretch like a hammock between your pubic bone at the front, your tailbone at the back and your two sit bones at the sides. There are three openings passing through this hammock, the urethra, the vagina and the anus. The outer layers wrap around these openings like little rings and stop you from leaking, even when you cough, sneeze or laugh. The deep layer supports your organs, and right now in pregnancy it's also carrying your uterus, your baby, the amniotic fluid and the placenta. By the end of pregnancy that's quite a weight, and your pelvic floor is quietly doing this work every single day.

On top of that it stabilises your pelvis and lower spine, it's part of your core, and it plays a role in your sexuality and your pleasure. So it's much more than a muscle you only think about when something stops working.

Many women have learned that a good pelvic floor above all needs to be strong. Strength matters, of course. But a healthy muscle is one that can contract and then let go just as well. For some women the pelvic floor is actually too tight, because they sit a lot, live with a lot of stress or have got used to holding their belly and pelvis all the time. A pelvic floor that's constantly tense can show up as pain during sex, constipation or the feeling that you can never quite empty your bladder. And for birth, letting go is essential, because your baby has to pass through these muscle layers, and the more softly they can yield, the easier that journey becomes.

[your detail: how you only really got to know your own pelvic floor through your pregnancies]

So how do you find it? Sit upright on a chair and feel your sit bones. Then imagine gently closing the openings and drawing them a little inwards and upwards, as if you were picking up a blueberry with your pelvic floor. Your bottom, your thighs and your shoulders stay soft, and you keep breathing calmly. Many women hold their breath or bear down without noticing at first, which is completely normal and changes with practice. One thing I don't recommend, though, is regularly stopping the flow of urine on the toilet as a way of training your pelvic floor. That can disturb how your bladder empties.

Letting go is harder than engaging for a lot of women. With the pelvic floor breathing we practised, you consciously let it soften and drop as you breathe in, as if your pelvis were opening like a flower. As you breathe out, it gently lifts again. If you practise this connection again and again during pregnancy, your body will already know it well when you give birth.

I'd like to give you a few everyday tips as well. On the toilet, sit down properly instead of hovering over the seat, because when you hover your pelvic floor can't relax. A small stool under your feet makes bowel movements easier, and try to avoid straining. When you lift something heavy, breathe out as you come up and gently engage your pelvic floor at the same time. And if you leak a few drops when you cough or sneeze during pregnancy, that's common, but it isn't something you simply have to live with. Mention it to your midwife or your doctor, because pelvic floor physiotherapy can make a big difference even now.

[pause]

A word on perineal massage, which I mentioned briefly in the session. The perineum is the tissue between the vagina and the anus, and it stretches a great deal during birth. Studies show that regular perineal massage from around 34 weeks can reduce the risk of tears that need stitches, especially with a first baby. It's best to have your midwife show you the technique and to check with her first whether anything speaks against it for you, such as an infection or varicose veins in the vulva. Part of the benefit is getting to know the sensation of stretching and learning to stay soft within it.

In the movement video for this session I'll guide you through all the exercises again. It includes finding your pelvic floor while seated, the side-lying Clamshell, rocking on all fours and the supported squat, Malasana. In the squat, make sure you're well supported, for example on a block or a cushion. If your baby is in a breech position towards the end of pregnancy, please ask your midwife whether deep squats are right for you at the moment. In your workbook there's a little drawing of the pelvic floor and space for your observations, because it really helps to be able to picture it.

Your task until next time is to take ten breaths twice a day, deliberately letting go each time you breathe in. You can do this sitting at your desk, at a red light in the car or on the sofa in the evening.

[pause, smile]

If you take just one thing away today, let it be this soft letting go as you breathe in. Feel free to start the movement video now, and we'll practise it together once more.

[Finding your pelvic floor, seated · 8 repetitions]
Sit tall on a chair and feel your two sit bones. Breathe in and let everything soften. As you breathe out, imagine drawing your sit bones gently towards each other and lift your pelvic floor a little inwards and upwards, as if you were picking up a blueberry. With the next breath in, let go completely. Letting go is just as important as engaging.
[Glutes, thighs and belly stay relaxed, only the pelvic floor works.]

[Clamshell, side-lying · 2 × 12 each side]
Lie on your side, head resting on your arm, knees bent and heels in line with your bottom. As you breathe out, open your top knee while your feet stay together. As you breathe in, close slowly. Your pelvis doesn't roll back.
[Strengthens the side of the hip that keeps your pelvis stable.]

[Rocking on all fours · 1 minute]
Come onto all fours and rock very gently forwards and backwards. With every breath out, feel your pelvic floor lift a little, and with every breath in, feel it widen.
[Helpful if you feel downward pressure, because in this position your baby puts less weight on your pelvic floor.]

[Supported squat (Malasana) · 3 × 5 breaths]
Stand in front of a chair or sit on a low stool, feet wide apart and turned slightly out. Sink down low and hold on securely. Breathe into your pelvis and with every breath in let your pelvic floor become soft and wide. This is where we practise the letting go you need for the birth.
[If your baby is breech after week 35 or you have pain at your pubic bone, practise this seated only.]

[Breathwork · Pelvic floor breathing]
Sit comfortably or stay on all fours. Breathe in through your nose and let your belly, your ribs and your pelvic floor widen, like a flower opening. Breathe out through slightly parted lips and feel your pelvic floor lift very gently.

We take ten breaths. In and soften, out and gently lift. If you get tired, simply stay with breathing in and letting go.

[Meditation · Visualisation: opening]
Lie on your side and make yourself comfortable with pillows. Close your eyes if you like.

Imagine a flower in a colour you love. It is still completely closed. With every breath out it opens one petal, very slowly, without you having to do anything.

Your body may open in the same way when the time comes. Not with force, but at its own pace. Stay with this flower for a few more breaths.

[CLOSING]
If you only take one thing home today, let it be letting go as you breathe in. It will help you so much during the birth.

[Talking Head · direkt in die Kamera · ca. 9 Min.]

Hallo, schön, dass du da bist. In unserer letzten Stunde ging es um deinen Rücken, und ich weiß, dass dieses Thema viele Schwangere jeden Tag begleitet. Ungefähr zwei von drei Frauen haben irgendwann in der Schwangerschaft Rücken- oder Beckenschmerzen. Wenn du dazugehörst, bist du also alles andere als allein, und trotzdem möchte ich dir sagen, dass du das nicht einfach aushalten musst.

[kurze Pause]

Schauen wir uns zuerst an, woher die Beschwerden kommen. Dein Bauch zieht deinen Schwerpunkt nach vorn, und viele Frauen gleichen das mit einem stärkeren Hohlkreuz aus. Gleichzeitig sind deine Bänder durch die Schwangerschaftshormone weicher, auch die kräftigen Bänder rund um dein Kreuzbein und deine Iliosakralgelenke, also die Verbindung zwischen Wirbelsäule und Becken. Damit das Becken trotzdem stabil bleibt, müssen manche Muskeln mehr arbeiten als vorher, und wenn sie ermüden, spürst du das als Ziehen oder Brennen im unteren Rücken. Dazu kommt, dass die geraden Bauchmuskeln sich dehnen, damit dein Baby Platz hat, und dadurch etwas weniger stützen können.

Manchmal strahlt der Schmerz ins Gesäß oder hinten ins Bein aus. Das nennen viele Ischias, und tatsächlich kommt es in der Schwangerschaft meist vom Becken und von den Iliosakralgelenken, seltener direkt vom Ischiasnerv. Bitte lass dich ärztlich untersuchen, wenn du Taubheit oder Kribbeln im Bein spürst, wenn dein Bein schwächer wird oder du Probleme hast, die Blase oder den Darm zu kontrollieren. Und ein Rückenschmerz, der in regelmäßigen Abständen kommt und geht, kann auch eine Wehe sein. Wenn du dir unsicher bist, ruf lieber einmal mehr bei deiner Hebamme oder im Kreißsaal an.

Wenn es vorn am Schambein schmerzt, betrifft das meist die Symphyse. Die beiden Hälften deines Beckens sind dort durch einen Knorpel verbunden, und der wird in der Schwangerschaft ebenfalls etwas lockerer. Viele Frauen spüren das besonders beim Treppensteigen, beim Anziehen einer Hose im Stehen, beim Aussteigen aus dem Auto oder wenn sie sich im Bett umdrehen. Für die Symphyse gilt eine einfache Regel: Bewegungen, bei denen die Beine weit auseinandergehen oder das Gewicht nur auf einem Bein lastet, sind eher ungünstig. Du ziehst deine Hose deshalb im Sitzen an, du steigst Stufe für Stufe die Treppe hinauf und schwingst beim Aussteigen aus dem Auto beide Beine gemeinsam hinaus. Ein Beckengurt kann zusätzlich Halt geben, und eine Physiotherapeutin, die sich mit Schwangerschaft auskennt, ist hier eine große Hilfe.

[dein Detail: ein Moment aus deinen Schwangerschaften, in dem Rücken oder Becken dich gebremst haben]

Was wirklich hilft, und das sage ich aus Überzeugung, ist Kraft. Wenn deine Beine kräftig sind, kannst du aus der Hocke hochkommen und Dinge heben, ohne dass dein unterer Rücken die ganze Arbeit übernimmt. Ein starker oberer Rücken hält deine Schultern und deinen Brustkorb aufrecht, gerade jetzt, wo deine Brust schwerer wird und du später dein Baby viele Stunden am Tag tragen und stillen wirst. Und eine stabile Mitte, die mit dem Atem zusammenarbeitet, gibt deinem Becken Halt.

Darum haben wir die Kniebeuge an der Wand geübt, das Rudern mit dem Band, den Bird Dog im Vierfüßlerstand und den Seitstütz auf dem Knie. Bei allen Übungen nutzt du die Kraft-Atmung: Du atmest ein, bevor du die Bewegung beginnst, und atmest bei der Anstrengung aus, während du sanft den Beckenboden und den tiefen Bauch mitnimmst. So schützt du deinen Beckenboden und deine Bauchmitte vor zu viel Druck. Achte dabei auch auf deinen Bauch. Wenn sich in der Mitte eine Wölbung oder ein Grat bildet, dann ist die Übung im Moment zu schwer für dich, und wir machen sie kleiner oder leichter. Zum Schluss haben wir den Hüftbeuger im Halbkniestand gedehnt, denn wenn er durch viel Sitzen verkürzt ist, zieht er dein Becken zusätzlich ins Hohlkreuz.

[Pause]

Neben dem Training bewirken die kleinen Gewohnheiten im Alltag am meisten. Aus dem Liegen stehst du über die Seite auf: Du drehst dich mit angewinkelten Beinen auf die Seite, schiebst dich mit den Armen hoch und lässt die Beine dabei langsam aus dem Bett gleiten. Das schont deinen Rücken und deine Bauchmitte, und du wirst es auch nach der Geburt im Wochenbett brauchen. Wenn du etwas hebst, etwa ein Geschwisterkind oder den Wäschekorb, gehst du in die Knie, hältst die Last nah am Körper und atmest beim Hochkommen aus. Und beim Umdrehen im Bett hältst du die Knie zusammen und drehst dich als Ganzes, das entlastet vor allem die Symphyse.

Zum Schlafen ist die Seitenlage am angenehmsten, mit einem Kissen zwischen den Knien und einem kleinen unter dem Bauch. Ab etwa der 28. Woche wird ohnehin empfohlen, auf der Seite einzuschlafen, weil in der Rückenlage die Gebärmutter auf große Blutgefäße drücken kann. Wenn du nachts auf dem Rücken aufwachst, musst du dir keine Sorgen machen, dreh dich einfach wieder auf die Seite.

Im Bewegungsvideo zu dieser Einheit zeige ich dir jede Übung noch einmal Schritt für Schritt, mit leichteren und etwas fordernderen Varianten, damit du deinen Weg findest. Im Workbook findest du eine kleine Übersicht zu den Alltagsbewegungen zum Ausdrucken, die du dir an den Kühlschrank hängen kannst.

Deine Aufgabe für die kommenden Wochen ist, an drei Tagen pro Woche Kniebeugen und Rudern zu üben, jeweils zweimal zehn Wiederholungen. Das dauert keine zehn Minuten, und schon nach wenigen Wochen wirst du merken, dass dir manches im Alltag leichter fällt.

[Pause, lächeln]

Kraft und Weichheit gehören zusammen, und ein kräftiger Körper kann sich viel leichter entspannen. Starte jetzt gern das Bewegungsvideo, ich bin bei jeder Wiederholung mit dabei.

[Talking head · straight to camera · approx. 9 min.]

Hi, it's lovely to have you here. Our last session was all about your back, and I know this is something many pregnant women live with every day. Around two out of three women have back or pelvic pain at some point in pregnancy. So if that's you, you are far from alone, but I still want you to know that you don't have to just put up with it.

[short pause]

Let's first look at where the discomfort comes from. Your belly pulls your centre of gravity forward, and many women compensate by arching their lower back more. At the same time your pregnancy hormones make your ligaments softer, including the strong ligaments around your sacrum and your sacroiliac joints, where your spine meets your pelvis. To keep your pelvis stable anyway, some muscles have to work harder than before, and when they get tired you feel it as a pulling or burning sensation in your lower back. On top of that, the long abdominal muscles down the front of your belly stretch to make room for your baby, so they can offer a little less support.

Sometimes the pain radiates into your buttock or down the back of your leg. Many people call that sciatica, and in pregnancy it usually comes from the pelvis and the sacroiliac joints, less often from the sciatic nerve itself. Please get checked by a doctor if you feel numbness or tingling in your leg, if your leg becomes weaker, or if you have trouble controlling your bladder or bowel. And back pain that comes and goes at regular intervals can also be a contraction. If you're unsure, don't hesitate to call your midwife or the labour ward.

Pain at the front, right over your pubic bone, usually involves the pubic symphysis. The two halves of your pelvis are joined there by cartilage, and it also loosens a bit in pregnancy. Many women notice it most when climbing stairs, pulling on trousers while standing, getting out of the car or turning over in bed. For your symphysis there's one simple rule: movements where your legs go wide apart or all your weight rests on one leg tend to aggravate it. So you put your trousers on sitting down, take the stairs one step at a time and swing both legs out of the car together. A pelvic support belt can give you extra stability, and a physiotherapist who specialises in pregnancy can help enormously here.

[your detail: a moment in your pregnancies when your back or pelvis slowed you down]

What really helps, and I truly believe this, is strength. When your legs are strong, you can come up from a squat and lift things without your lower back doing all the work. A strong upper back keeps your shoulders and chest upright, especially now that your breasts are getting heavier and you'll soon be carrying and feeding your baby for hours every day. And a stable core that works together with your breath gives your pelvis support.

That's why we practised the wall squat, the band row, Bird Dog on all fours and the kneeling side plank. In every exercise you use breathing for strength: you breathe in before you start the movement and breathe out during the effort, gently drawing in your pelvic floor and deep belly as you go. This protects your pelvic floor and your core from too much pressure. Keep an eye on your belly as well. If you see a dome or a ridge forming down the middle, the exercise is too much for you right now, and we make it smaller or easier. At the end we stretched the hip flexors in a half-kneeling position, because when they're tight from lots of sitting, they pull your pelvis even further into that arch.

[pause]

Beyond training, small everyday habits make the biggest difference. When you get up from lying down, roll onto your side first: bend your knees, turn onto your side, push yourself up with your arms and let your legs slide slowly off the bed. This protects your back and your core, and you'll need it again after the birth in the postpartum weeks. When you lift something, an older sibling perhaps or the laundry basket, bend your knees, keep the load close to your body and breathe out as you come up. And when you turn over in bed, keep your knees together and roll as one unit, which takes a lot of strain off the front of your pelvis.

For sleeping, lying on your side is usually the most comfortable, with a pillow between your knees and a small one under your belly. From around 28 weeks it's recommended to go to sleep on your side anyway, because when you lie on your back, your uterus can press on major blood vessels. If you wake up on your back during the night, there's no need to worry, just roll back onto your side.

In the movement video for this session I'll show you each exercise again step by step, with easier and slightly more challenging options so you can find your own way. In your workbook there's a little printable overview of the everyday movements that you can stick on your fridge.

Your task for the coming weeks is squats and rows, two sets of ten on three days a week. It takes less than ten minutes, and within a few weeks you'll notice that everyday life feels a little easier.

[pause, smile]

Strength and softness belong together, and a strong body finds it much easier to relax. Feel free to start the movement video now, I'll be with you for every rep.

[Talking head · straight to camera · approx. 8 min.]

Hi, lovely to have you here. Birth is slowly getting closer, and in our session we looked at which positions might help you and how your birth partner can support you. Here I'd like to go a little deeper and share a few thoughts that can give you confidence in these last weeks.

[short pause]

When we think of birth, most of us picture a scene from a film: a woman lying on her back in bed with her legs drawn up. That position is practical for doctors and midwives because they can see well and step in if needed, and sometimes it's also the right one for medical reasons. For many women, though, it isn't the most comfortable, because on your back your sacrum is pressed against the bed and can't move backwards. Your pelvis isn't a rigid ring. When you stand, kneel, go onto all fours or squat, your sacrum can move back a little and your pelvis opens slightly wider, at the top or the bottom, depending on the position.

Upright positions also use gravity, which gently guides your baby downwards. Studies show that women in upright positions often have a somewhat shorter first stage and need an epidural less often. Just as important is that you keep moving. When a position stops feeling good, you change it, and your body will often show you quite intuitively what it needs.

Side-lying, by the way, is a wonderful position for gathering your strength in between, and even with an epidural you can turn onto your side or onto all fours with some help. Rest is as much a part of birth as movement.

[your detail: which position helped you in your own births]

Now to your birth partner, because their role is bigger than many partners realise. A lot of them feel helpless during labour because they can't take the pain away. Yet they can make an incredible difference. The sacral massage we practised is a calm, circular movement with the flat of the hand or the heel of the hand on the flat bone just above your bottom. Many women find warm hands right there a great relief, especially when they feel the contractions in their back. For the hip squeeze, your partner places their hands on the sides of your pelvis and presses firmly towards the middle during a contraction. Warmth on your lower back, like a heat pack or a warm shower, can help you relax even more.

Often the most valuable thing is something very quiet, though. Your partner can remind you of your breath when you lose your rhythm, simply by breathing calmly alongside you. They can hand you water, dim the lights, answer questions for you and make sure you're left undisturbed. Talk beforehand about what you'd like from them, and try out the techniques a few times at home.

In the session we also practised releasing your jaw and hands. It sounds minor, but it's very effective. Many midwives notice that a loose mouth and a soft jaw help the pelvic floor soften too. If you notice yourself clenching your teeth or making fists, let your lower jaw drop and your fingers soften as you breathe out. Your partner is very welcome to remind you.

[pause]

Breathing down is about the second stage. Instead of holding your breath and pushing until you're red in the face, you let a long exhale flow downwards towards your pelvis and work with the urge your body already has. Sometimes your midwife will guide you differently for good reasons, and then you follow her. It's simply good to know both options.

And finally, your birth preferences. I'd encourage you to write them down, ideally on a single page so the team in the labour room can read them quickly. What would you like to try, which positions, water, music, low lighting? How do you feel about pain relief? What matters to you after the birth, perhaps that first skin-to-skin moment on your chest or letting the cord stop pulsing before it's cut? Birth can't be planned, and a lot may turn out differently. Your wishes are still valuable, because they show everyone what feels right for you, and because writing them down helps you get to know yourself even better.

In the movement video for this session I'll take you through the birth position flow again at a calm pace, and I'll show your birth partner the sacral massage and the hip squeeze so you can practise together. In your workbook you'll find a template for your birth preferences and a page of affirmations.

Your task is to choose your favourite affirmation, write it down and put it somewhere you'll see it every day, on the bathroom mirror or next to your bed.

[pause, smile]

You don't have to perform during birth, you can let your body and your baby lead the way. Feel free to bring your birth partner in now and start the movement video together.

[Talking head · straight to camera · approx. 8 min.]

Hi, I'm so glad you're here. Our second session was all about your pelvic floor, and because this topic raises so many questions, I'd like to go into it more deeply here, without any rush.

[short pause]

Your pelvic floor is a layer of muscle and connective tissue that closes off your pelvis from below like a hammock. It supports the organs in your pelvis and keeps you in control of your bladder and bowels. It never works alone, though. It's closely connected with your diaphragm and your deep abdominal muscles, and that's exactly why breathing plays such a big role in our work together.

During a vaginal birth, the pelvic floor stretches to several times its normal length so that your baby can pass through. Sometimes that leads to tears, an episiotomy or small injuries you can't see from the outside. After a caesarean that stretch didn't happen, yet your pelvic floor still carried a growing weight for nine months, and the pregnancy hormones softened the tissue. So everything I'm telling you today applies to every mother, however your baby came into the world.

The good news is that your pelvic floor can be trained like any other muscle. It needs two kinds of training, and we practised both in the live session. The quick squeezes train its reflexes, its ability to close in a flash when you cough or sneeze. The long holds, where you hold for five to ten seconds, build endurance, so that it supports you well when you're standing or carrying for a long time.

Letting go is just as important as tightening, by the way. A pelvic floor that is tense all the time isn't automatically strong, and some women actually feel after the birth that they can't fully relax it any more. So after every squeeze, make a point of consciously letting go and feeling your pelvic floor soften downwards.

[pause]

You may be wondering whether you're doing it right. It's one of the questions I hear most often, and it's a fair one, because you can't see your pelvic floor. A helpful image is to gently draw your sit bones towards each other as you breathe out, and then let your pelvic floor rise like a lift going up one floor. Your bottom and thighs stay relaxed, and you keep breathing calmly. If you're unsure, an assessment with a pelvic health physiotherapist is really worth it. She can feel exactly how your muscles are working and show you what to pay attention to.

Now let's talk about everyday life, because that's where most of it happens. You lift your baby what feels like a hundred times a day, you carry the car seat and the laundry basket, and every time, pressure builds in your abdomen and pushes down on your pelvic floor. So the most important habit I'd like to give you is this one: breathe out before you lift, gently engage your pelvic floor as you do, and only then come up. At first you'll have to think about it, but after a few weeks it happens almost on its own.

The Knack works in a very similar way. Just before you cough or sneeze, you briefly tighten your pelvic floor, and this small habit alone can noticeably reduce leaking in those moments. When you get up from lying down, keep rolling onto your side first for the next few weeks. You can support your pelvic floor on the toilet too, by not straining. A small stool under your feet puts your bowel in a better position, and drinking enough helps prevent the constipation that is so common after birth.

[calmer tone]

I want to be honest with you here, because this is talked about far too little. In the first weeks after birth it's common to leak a little or to feel heaviness in your pelvic floor. But if that's still the case after about six to eight weeks, if you feel pressure or a bulge in your vagina, if you find it hard to hold in wind or stool, or if sex is painful, please get yourself checked. These are not things you simply have to live with because you're a mother. Pelvic health physiotherapy can make a huge difference here, and the earlier you start, the better. Please also mention it openly at your postnatal check with your doctor, even if it feels awkward, because she hears these questions every single day. [your detail: how this was for you, if you'd like to share]

I'd also like to say something about the meditation at the end of our session, compassion for your own body. Many women feel disappointed in their pelvic floor after birth, or ashamed that it doesn't work the way it used to. I understand that feeling well, and yet I'd like to invite you to see it in a different light. This muscle helped carry your baby for nine months, and perhaps it also made way for your baby to come into the world. It deserves patience, and it responds remarkably well to a few minutes of attention a day.

[pause, smile]

Your home practice is deliberately small: ten quick squeezes and five long holds, three times a day. That takes barely two minutes, and you can fit it in anywhere, for example while you're feeding or waiting at a red light. Some women stick a little coloured dot on the mirror as a reminder.

In the movement video for this session we'll do the quick squeezes and long holds together, along with the glute bridge and the clamshell, which strengthen your glutes and support your pelvic floor from the outside. In your workbook you'll find the most important everyday tips to read again and space for your notes.

Take all the time you need. I'm looking forward to our next session.

[Talking head · straight to camera · approx. 8 min.]

Hi, it's lovely to have you back. In our third session we focused on your midline, and because there are so many myths and so much worry around diastasis recti, I'd like to explain in more detail what has happened in your belly and what you can do for it now.

[short pause]

Your rectus abdominis, the muscle people sometimes call the six-pack, runs in two bands from your breastbone down to your pubic bone. In the middle the two bands are joined by a seam of connective tissue called the linea alba. During pregnancy, hormones soften this seam and your growing baby stretches it, so the two bands of muscle move apart. That's a clever adaptation of your body, because otherwise your baby simply wouldn't have had room. By the end of pregnancy almost every woman has a diastasis, so you're in very good company.

After the birth, the gap starts to narrow on its own for many women over the first weeks and months. For some it stays for longer, especially after several pregnancies or after twins. That's no reason to worry either, because with targeted training the midline can recover really well.

[pause]

Now comes the point that matters most to me. Many women measure their gap with their fingers and then become completely fixed on that one number. The width only tells part of the story, though. What matters much more is how the tissue feels deep down when you engage your abdominal muscles. If your fingers meet something firm when you lift your head, something that springs back a little like a trampoline, then your midline can transfer force, even if two fingers still fit in the gap. If your fingers sink in deeply and everything feels soft, your midline needs more focused work. So what we're aiming for is a midline that can take load, and for that the gap doesn't always have to close completely.

The key to this is your transverse abdominal muscle, the transversus abdominis. It lies very deep and wraps around your belly like a corset. When it engages, it brings tension to the linea alba and gives your midline support. It works closely with your pelvic floor, and that's exactly why we link it with your breath in every exercise. With zip-up breathing, you imagine closing a zip from your pubic bone up to your belly button as you breathe out, and you feel your lower belly gently drawing in.

[calmer tone]

There's one sign I'd really like you to keep in mind, and that's coning, sometimes called doming. If your midline bulges up during an exercise like a little tent or a ridge, the pressure in your belly is greater than your midline can hold right now. That's nothing to panic about, and it doesn't mean you've damaged anything. It's simply a cue to make the exercise smaller or to breathe out more deliberately. Over time you'll notice that you can do exercises without coning that were too hard for you at the beginning.

We're leaving out classic sit-ups and crunches for now, because they put a lot of forward pressure on the midline. Later on, when your midline holds well, they're welcome back in your training, because no exercise is forbidden forever. What counts is always whether your body can handle it well at this moment.

And in everyday life? Keep getting out of bed by rolling onto your side, instead of hauling yourself up as if you were doing a sit-up. Breathe out when you lift, and notice whether you keep arching your lower back and pushing your belly forward while you carry your baby. Whenever you feel your belly pressing forward noticeably during everyday movements, that's a good moment to briefly switch on your deep abdominal muscle.

You may also have heard of support belts or kinesiology tape. They can feel pleasant in the first weeks and give you some support, but they don't replace training. It's best to ask your midwife or your physiotherapist whether something like that makes sense for you.

If the gap has hardly changed even after several months of consistent training, please get it assessed, for example by a physiotherapist who specialises in the postnatal period. And if you notice a bulge in your midline that hurts or no longer goes back on its own, please see your doctor soon, because it could be a hernia.

[pause, smile]

Your home practice is heel slides and toe taps, two sets of ten each, on four days a week. That sounds unspectacular, yet these calm, controlled movements are exactly what teaches your deep abdominal muscle to hold your midline while your legs are moving. [your detail: how long it took you until your midline felt stable again]

In the movement video for this session we'll go through all the exercises together, from the transversus activation through heel slides and toe taps to the modified dead bug and core breathing on all fours. In your workbook you can compare your self-check result with the one from the beginning and note every few weeks how your midline feels.

Be patient with your midline. I'm looking forward to seeing you next time.

[Transversus activation (deep abdominal muscle) · 10 repetitions]
Lie on your back with your knees bent. Breathe in and let your belly soften. Breathe out and draw your navel gently towards your spine, as if you were tightening a belt by one notch. Your pelvic floor lifts with it. Hold briefly and let go.
[Your back stays still on the mat.]

[Heel slides · 2 × 10 each side]
Stay on your back. As you breathe out, activate your core and slowly slide one heel along the floor until the leg is almost straight. As you breathe in, draw it back in. Then the other side.
[It's easier in socks on a smooth floor.]

[Toe taps · 2 × 10 each side]
On your back, lift both legs one after the other into tabletop, knees above your hips. As you breathe out, lower one foot and tap the floor with your toes. As you breathe in, come back. Your lower back stays still.
[Too hard? Keep one foot on the floor.]

[Dead Bug (modified) · 2 × 6 each side]
Stay in tabletop and reach your arms up to the ceiling. As you breathe out, move your right arm back and your left leg forward, only as far as your belly stays flat. Come back as you breathe in, then the other side.
[Watch for coning, and if you see it, make the movement smaller.]

[Core breathing on all fours · 8 breaths]
Come onto all fours. Breathe in and let your belly hang towards the floor. Breathe out and draw it gently inwards and upwards, without rounding your back.
[Gravity makes the exercise a little more demanding here.]

[Breathwork · Zip-up breathing]
Lie on your back with your hands on your belly. Breathe in and let your belly widen. Breathe out slowly and imagine slowly doing up a zip from your pubic bone to your breastbone. First your pelvic floor lifts, then your lower belly flattens, then your midline closes all the way up to your ribs.

As you breathe in, undo the zip again. Ten breaths.

[Meditation · Relaxation lying on your back]
Place a pillow under your knees and let your legs become completely heavy. Your arms rest loosely beside you, palms facing up.

Feel your belly rising and falling with every breath. It carried your baby and can now heal in peace. With every breath out your body sinks a little deeper into the floor. Stay like this as long as you like.

[CLOSING]
Your core needs patience, not hardness. Every calm repetition takes you further.

Lie on your side with your knees bent and stacked, arms long in front of you. As you breathe in, open your top arm like a book to the other side and follow it with your eyes. Your knees stay together. As you breathe out, close the book again.
[Opens your upper spine, which tends to round from feeding.]

[No band? Do a standing bent-over row with two water bottles.]

Stand in a doorway and place your forearm against the frame at shoulder height. Take a small step forward until you feel a stretch at the front of your chest. Breathe calmly and change sides.
[Ideal straight after feeding.]

Stand hip-width apart and hold your baby or a weight close in front of your chest. As you breathe in, sit back and down. As you breathe out, lift your pelvic floor and come up through your heels.

Stand with your back against the wall, feet a little in front of it. Place your arms and the backs of your hands against the wall in a U shape. As you breathe in, slide your arms slowly up, and as you breathe out, slide them back down, keeping your shoulders away from your ears.
[Only as far as your arms can stay on the wall.]

Sit comfortably. Breathe in and draw your shoulders up to your ears. Hold briefly. Breathe out audibly through your mouth and let your shoulders drop down heavily.

You can take this little pause anywhere, on the sofa, while feeding or while your baby sleeps.

Close your eyes or lower your gaze. First feel your feet on the floor. Then your breath, without changing it. Then your shoulders, and let them drop a little. Then your face, your forehead, your jaw, and let everything soften.

[Talking Head · direkt in die Kamera · ca. 8 Min.]

Hallo, schön, dass du wieder da bist. In unserer fünften Einheit haben wir einen richtigen Schritt nach vorne gemacht und echte Kraft aufgebaut. Ich möchte dir hier erklären, wie du die Belastung klug steigerst und woran du merkst, dass dein Körper noch etwas mehr Zeit braucht.

[kurze Pause]

Wenn wir über Training nach der Geburt sprechen, denken viele zuerst an den Bauch oder an das Gewicht. Mir geht es um etwas anderes, nämlich um die Kraft, die du jeden Tag brauchst. Überleg einmal, was dein Alltag gerade von dir verlangt. Du hebst ein Baby, das jede Woche schwerer wird, vom Boden und aus dem Autositz. Du gehst mit ihm auf dem Arm in die Hocke, um etwas aufzuheben, du trägst es Treppen hinauf und wiegst es abends in den Schlaf, oft eine halbe Stunde lang. Das ist körperliche Arbeit, und dein Körper verdient es, darauf vorbereitet zu sein.

Die Übungen, die wir gemacht haben, bilden genau diese Alltagsbewegungen ab. In der Kniebeuge stecken das Hinsetzen und Aufheben, und der Ausfallschritt rückwärts entspricht dem Hinknien und Aufstehen, wenn du dein Baby zum Beispiel auf der Krabbeldecke versorgst. Die einbeinige Schulterbrücke kräftigt deine Gesäßmuskeln und stabilisiert dein Becken, was deinen unteren Rücken und deinen Beckenboden entlastet. Mit dem Seitstütz auf dem Knie trainierst du die seitliche Rumpfmuskulatur, die dich hält, wenn du dein Baby auf einer Hüfte trägst, und das Rudern mit Band stärkt deinen oberen Rücken für all das Halten und Tragen.

[Pause]

Jetzt zum wichtigsten Teil, dem Steigern. Dein Gewebe passt sich an Belastung an, aber es braucht dafür Zeit, und Bindegewebe ist dabei deutlich langsamer als Muskulatur. Deshalb gehen wir in kleinen Schritten vor. Zuerst festigen wir die saubere Ausführung, und wenn sie sich leicht anfühlt, kommen mehr Wiederholungen oder eine schwierigere Variante dazu. Lieber hörst du eine Wiederholung zu früh auf, als eine zu viel zu machen.

Dabei helfen dir die Warnzeichen, die ich dir gerne noch einmal ausführlich erkläre. Das erste ist ein Druck- oder Schweregefühl, als ob etwas im Becken nach unten drängt. Ein weiteres ist Urinverlust während der Übung. Dann gibt es das Coning, bei dem sich deine Bauchmitte zeltartig nach oben wölbt, und schließlich Schmerz, sei es im Rücken, im Becken, an der Narbe oder in den Gelenken. Wenn eines dieser Zeichen auftaucht, sagt dir dein Körper, dass diese Übung in dieser Form im Moment noch zu viel ist. Dann machst du sie leichter oder mit weniger Wiederholungen, und manchmal hilft es schon, bewusster auszuatmen, während du dich anstrengst.

Dieses Ausatmen in der Anstrengung, das wir bei der Atemübung geübt haben, ist einer der wirksamsten Helfer überhaupt. Wenn du beim Hochkommen aus der Kniebeuge ausatmest und dabei Beckenboden und Bauchmitte sanft mitnimmst, verteilt sich der Druck im Bauchraum besser, und dein Beckenboden muss weniger dagegenhalten. Die Luft anzuhalten und zu pressen geschieht ganz automatisch, sobald es schwer wird, und deshalb lohnt es sich, das Ausatmen so lange zu üben, bis es dir selbstverständlich geworden ist.

[ruhiger Ton]

Ich weiß, wie frustrierend es sein kann, einen Schritt zurückzugehen, gerade wenn du das Gefühl hast, endlich voranzukommen. [dein Detail: ein Moment, in dem du selbst geduldiger mit deinem Körper sein musstest] Trotzdem möchte ich dir zeigen, wie ich das sehe. Training nach der Geburt verläuft nie in einer geraden Linie. Es gibt Tage, an denen du nach einer schlechten Nacht kaum Kraft hast, und Tage, an denen alles leicht geht. Vielleicht kommt auch dein Zyklus zurück, und auch er beeinflusst, wie belastbar du dich fühlst. Wenn du an einem Tag die leichtere Variante wählst, hast du nichts verloren. Du hast deinem Körper genau das gegeben, was er an diesem Tag verarbeiten konnte, und auf diese Weise wirst du langfristig stark.

Es gibt allerdings Situationen, in denen du mit dem Steigern bitte wartest und das Gespräch mit deiner Hebamme, deiner Ärztin oder einer Beckenboden-Physiotherapeutin suchst. Das gilt, wenn Beschwerden trotz leichterer Übungen über Wochen bestehen bleiben oder wenn deine Kaiserschnittnarbe nach dem Training schmerzt oder sich verändert.

[Pause, lächeln]

Deine Hausaufgabe ist ein kleines Kraftprogramm von zehn Minuten aus Kniebeugen, Brücke und Rudern, dreimal pro Woche. Du kannst dein Baby gern mit einbeziehen und es neben dich auf die Decke legen, oder du nutzt eines seiner Schläfchen am Tag. Wenn dein Baby größer wird, kannst du es bei der Kniebeuge auch auf dem Arm halten, und dann wächst dein Trainingsgewicht ganz von selbst mit.

Im Bewegungsvideo zu dieser Einheit machen wir das ganze Programm gemeinsam, mit leichteren und schwereren Varianten, sodass du immer die passende für dich findest. In deinem Workbook findest du die Warnzeichen noch einmal zum Nachlesen und Platz, um festzuhalten, wie sich deine Wiederholungen entwickeln.

Du bist schon so viel kräftiger geworden, und ich freue mich darauf, das beim nächsten Mal wieder zu sehen. Bis bald.

[Talking head · straight to camera · approx. 8 min.]

Hi, it's good to see you again. In our fifth session we took a real step forward and started building proper strength. Here I'd like to explain how to increase the load wisely and how to tell when your body still needs a bit more time.

[short pause]

When we talk about training after birth, many people think first about their belly or their weight. What I care about is something else, the strength you need every single day. Think about what your everyday life is asking of you right now. You lift a baby who gets heavier every week, from the floor and out of the car seat. You squat down with your baby in your arms to pick something up, you carry them upstairs and rock them to sleep in the evening, often for half an hour. That's physical work, and your body deserves to be prepared for it.

The exercises we did mirror exactly these everyday movements. The squat is sitting down and picking things up, and the reverse lunge is kneeling down and getting up again, for example when you're looking after your baby on the play mat. The single-leg glute bridge strengthens your glutes and stabilises your pelvis, which takes strain off your lower back and your pelvic floor. The kneeling side plank trains the muscles along the side of your trunk that hold you when you carry your baby on one hip, and the band row strengthens your upper back for all that holding and carrying.

[pause]

Now to the most important part, progressing. Your tissues adapt to load, but they need time to do it, and connective tissue adapts much more slowly than muscle. That's why we move forward in small steps. First we make the technique solid, and once it feels easy, we add more repetitions or a harder variation. It's better to stop one repetition too early than to do one too many.

The warning signs help you with this, and I'd like to go through them again in more detail. The first is a feeling of pressure or heaviness, as if something in your pelvis is pushing down. Another is leaking urine during the exercise. Then there's coning, where your midline bulges up like a tent, and finally pain, whether in your back, your pelvis, your scar or your joints. If one of these signs shows up, your body is telling you that this exercise, in this form, is still too much right now. Then you make it easier or do fewer repetitions, and sometimes simply breathing out more deliberately while you work is enough.

Breathing out on the effort, which we practised in the breathing exercise, is one of the most effective helpers there is. When you breathe out as you rise from the squat and gently bring your pelvic floor and midline along with you, the pressure in your abdomen spreads more evenly and your pelvic floor has less to push against. Holding your breath and bearing down happens automatically as soon as things get heavy, so it's worth practising the exhale until it has become second nature.

[calmer tone]

I know how frustrating it can be to take a step back, especially when you feel you're finally making progress. [your detail: a time when you had to be more patient with your own body] Still, I'd like to share how I see it. Training after birth never follows a straight line. There are days when you have hardly any strength after a bad night, and days when everything feels easy. Your cycle may also be returning, and that affects how much your body can take as well. If you choose the easier variation on a given day, you haven't lost anything. You've given your body exactly what it could process that day, and that's how you become strong in the long run.

There are, however, situations where I'd ask you to hold off on progressing and talk to your midwife, your doctor or a pelvic health physiotherapist. That applies if symptoms stay for weeks even with easier exercises, or if your caesarean scar hurts or changes after training.

[pause, smile]

Your home practice is a short ten-minute strength routine of squats, bridges and rows, three times a week. You're welcome to include your baby and lay them next to you on the mat, or you can use one of their daytime naps. As your baby grows, you can also hold them in your arms for the squats, and then your training weight increases all by itself.

In the movement video for this session we'll go through the whole routine together, with easier and harder variations, so that you can always find the right one for you. In your workbook you'll find the warning signs again and space to note how your repetitions develop.

You've already become so much stronger, and I'm looking forward to seeing that again next time. See you soon.

[0:00 · ARRIVING]
Lovely to have you here. In this video we move together through the exercises from our session "Nervous system, sleep deprivation and mental load", so that you can repeat them at home whenever you like and at your own pace. Have a mat, a cushion and a blanket ready, and if anything does not feel good along the way, take a break or simply leave that exercise out.

[Shaking (somatic release) · 1 minute]
Stand and start shaking your hands, then your arms, your shoulders, your legs, until your whole body is shaking loosely. Feel free to let a sound out. Then stand completely still and notice how you feel.
[Releases tension through the body.]

[Swaying · 2 minutes]
Stand hip-width apart and shift your weight gently from one leg to the other, just as you do with your baby in your arms. Let your arms swing loosely with you. This swaying calms you too.
[Lovely with your eyes closed.]

[Neck and shoulder mobilisation · 1 minute]
Sit comfortably. Let your head sink slowly towards your right shoulder, breathe, and then to the left. Roll your shoulders slowly backwards. Everything very gently, without pressure.
[Small movements, lots of breath.]

[Child's Pose (Balasana) · 5 breaths]
Come onto all fours and sit back towards your heels, knees a little apart. Rest your forehead on your hands or a cushion. Breathe into your back.
[Put a cushion between your bottom and heels if your knees feel strained.]

[Legs up the wall (Viparita Karani) · 3 minutes]
Lie down with your bottom close to a wall and rest your legs up the wall. Your arms lie loosely beside you. Let the floor carry you.
[Soothing for heavy legs.]

[Breathwork · Long exhale and humming breath (Bhramari)]
Sit comfortably or stay lying down. Breathe in through your nose and count to four. Breathe out through your nose and hum softly, like a bee, as long as it feels comfortable.

Feel how the humming vibrates in your head and in your chest. This vibration calms your nervous system especially quickly. We hum ten times. You can do this with your baby in your arms too, many babies love it.

[Meditation · Yoga Nidra]
Lie down and make yourself completely comfortable, with a blanket over you if you like. For the next few minutes you don't have to do anything at all. If you fall asleep, that's all right.

First choose a short sentence for yourself, an intention, for example: I am enough. Say it to yourself three times in your thoughts.

Now I'll travel with you through your body. Your right hand, every single finger, your wrist, your forearm, your elbow, your shoulder. Your left hand, every finger, your arm, your shoulder. Your right foot, your toes, your heel, your leg. Your left foot, your toes, your leg. Your pelvis, your belly, your back. Your chest, your throat, your face.

Your whole body is lying here now, heavy and calm.

Imagine a place where you feel completely safe. Look around there, listen to what there is to hear, feel the air on your skin.

At the end, come back to your sentence once more and say it to yourself three times. Then slowly move your fingers and toes and come back at your own pace.

[CLOSING]
You are allowed to take breaks without earning them. They are simply part of it.
