Bring deine Aufmerksamkeit zu deinen Füßen. Lass sie schwer werden.

Deine Beine, schwer und warm.

Deine Hüften, die in den Boden sinken.

Dein Bauch, der sich von selbst hebt und senkt.

Deine Brust und dein Herz, das den ganzen Tag lang still für dich schlägt.

Deine Hände und deine Arme, lass sie schwer sein.

Deine Schultern, die nach unten schmelzen.

Dein Nacken und dein Kiefer. Lass deine Zähne ein wenig auseinandergehen.

Deine Augen, schwer in ihren Höhlen.

Deine Stirn, glatt und weit.

Dein ganzer Körper, gehalten vom Boden unter dir.

[Pause, etwa eine Minute Stille]

Lass uns jetzt in einem langsamen, beruhigenden Rhythmus atmen. Ein auf vier … und aus auf sechs.

[etwa zwei Minuten anleiten, leise zählen, dann Stille]

[Pause, etwa eine Minute Stille]

[24:00 · EINE FRAGE AUS DEM KREIS]

[Sprich hier leise. Wenn eine Frage im Chat oder in deiner Fragenliste steht, beantworte sie sanft. Wenn nicht, nimm diese:]

Eine Frage, die ich oft höre, lautet: „Was mache ich, wenn ich nachts meine Gedanken nicht abschalten kann?“

Kämpf nicht gegen sie an. Gedanken sind wie Wolken, und wenn man gegen sie kämpft, werden sie nur schwerer. Bemerk den Gedanken, sag dir leise „denken“ und kehr zu deinem Atem zurück. Ein auf vier, aus auf sechs. Immer wieder, so oft du es brauchst. Jedes Mal, wenn du zurückkommst, hast du es richtig gemacht.

[25:30 · ZURÜCKKOMMEN]

Komm jetzt langsam wieder zurück. Beweg deine Finger und deine Zehen.

Wenn du liegen bleiben und gleich einschlafen möchtest, darfst du das gern. Lass deine Kamera einfach aus und gleite hinüber.

Und wenn du noch einmal aufstehen musst, roll dich zuerst auf die Seite, bleib dort einen Atemzug lang liegen und komm langsam hoch.

[27:00 · EINE EINLADUNG]

[leise]

Wenn dir der heutige Abend gutgetan hat, komm zum nächsten Gathering. Die Gatherings sind kostenlos, und das Datum findest du auf moveciamovement.com.

Und wenn du solche Abende als Teil deines Lebens möchtest, mit tiefer Ruhe, Atemarbeit und sanfter Bewegung, immer dann, wenn du sie brauchst, dann öffnet meine Mindful Movement Method am 1. Dezember, und du kannst dir deinen Platz schon jetzt sichern.

[Wenn du heute Abend ein Angebot einblendest, dann jetzt und sag dazu:] Ich habe dir etwas eingeblendet. Schau es dir morgen an, wenn du ausgeruht bist. Es eilt nicht.

[28:30 · ABSCHLUSS]

Blas jetzt deine Kerze aus, oder lass deine Kräuter sicher in der Schale ruhen, bis sie ganz erloschen sind.

[deine ausblasen]

Leg deine Hände auf dein Herz.

Der Tag ist vorbei. Du hast dein Bestes gegeben. Du darfst jetzt ruhen.

Danke, dass du deinen Tag mit mir beendet hast.

Schlaft gut, ihr wilden Herzen. Gute Nacht.

[0:00 · ARRIVING]
Lovely to have you here. In this video we move together through the exercises from our session "Pelvic floor: engaging and letting go", so that you can repeat them at home whenever you like and at your own pace. Have a mat, a cushion and a blanket ready, and if anything does not feel good along the way, take a break or simply leave that exercise out.

[Finding your pelvic floor, seated · 8 repetitions]
Sit tall on a chair and feel your two sit bones. Breathe in and let everything soften. As you breathe out, imagine drawing your sit bones gently towards each other and lift your pelvic floor a little inwards and upwards, as if you were picking up a blueberry. With the next breath in, let go completely. Letting go is just as important as engaging.
[Glutes, thighs and belly stay relaxed, only the pelvic floor works.]

[Clamshell, side-lying · 2 × 12 each side]
Lie on your side, head resting on your arm, knees bent and heels in line with your bottom. As you breathe out, open your top knee while your feet stay together. As you breathe in, close slowly. Your pelvis doesn't roll back.
[Strengthens the side of the hip that keeps your pelvis stable.]

[Rocking on all fours · 1 minute]
Come onto all fours and rock very gently forwards and backwards. With every breath out, feel your pelvic floor lift a little, and with every breath in, feel it widen.
[Helpful if you feel downward pressure, because in this position your baby puts less weight on your pelvic floor.]

[Supported squat (Malasana) · 3 × 5 breaths]
Stand in front of a chair or sit on a low stool, feet wide apart and turned slightly out. Sink down low and hold on securely. Breathe into your pelvis and with every breath in let your pelvic floor become soft and wide. This is where we practise the letting go you need for the birth.
[If your baby is breech after week 35 or you have pain at your pubic bone, practise this seated only.]

[Breathwork · Pelvic floor breathing]
Sit comfortably or stay on all fours. Breathe in through your nose and let your belly, your ribs and your pelvic floor widen, like a flower opening. Breathe out through slightly parted lips and feel your pelvic floor lift very gently.

We take ten breaths. In and soften, out and gently lift. If you get tired, simply stay with breathing in and letting go.

[Meditation · Visualisation: opening]
Lie on your side and make yourself comfortable with pillows. Close your eyes if you like.

Imagine a flower in a colour you love. It is still completely closed. With every breath out it opens one petal, very slowly, without you having to do anything.

Your body may open in the same way when the time comes. Not with force, but at its own pace. Stay with this flower for a few more breaths.

[CLOSING]
If you only take one thing home today, let it be letting go as you breathe in. It will help you so much during the birth.

[Movement video · voice-over · you demonstrate, approx. 20 min.]

[0:00 · ARRIVING]
Lovely to have you here. In this video we move together through the exercises from our session "Relieving your back, strength for everyday life", so that you can repeat them at home whenever you like and at your own pace. Have a mat, a cushion and a blanket ready, and if anything does not feel good along the way, take a break or simply leave that exercise out.

[Wall squat · 2 × 10]
Stand with your back against the wall. Your feet are hip-width apart, a little in front of you. Breathe in and slide slowly down the wall, as if you were sitting down on a chair. As you breathe out, press up through your heels. Keep your knees in line with your toes.
[Only as deep as feels good.]

[Seated band row · 2 × 12]
Sit tall and loop the band around your feet. Hold the ends in your hands. As you breathe out, draw your elbows back and slide your shoulder blades gently towards each other. As you breathe in, let them move forward slowly. Your breastbone stays slightly lifted.
[Strengthens your upper back, which helps you carry the weight of your belly and breasts.]

[Bird Dog · 2 × 8 each side]
Come onto all fours. As you breathe out, reach your right arm forward and your left leg back, only as high as you can while keeping your back steady. Come back as you breathe in. Then change sides. Imagine a cup of tea on your back that must not fall over.
[If you have pain at your pubic bone, lift only the arm.]

[Kneeling side plank · 2 × 20 seconds each side]
Lie on your side and support yourself on your forearm, elbow under your shoulder. Your knees are bent. As you breathe out, lift your hips so that knees, hips and head form a line. Keep breathing calmly and hold. Then lower gently.
[If you have pain at your pubic bone, skip this and do clamshells instead.]

[Kneeling hip flexor stretch · 4 breaths each side]
Come into a half-kneeling position, right knee on a soft mat, left foot in front. Hold on to a chair. Gently move your pelvis forward until you feel a stretch at the front of your right hip. Breathe calmly and then change sides.
[Helps counter the arched lower back that comes with a growing belly.]

[Breathwork · Breathing for strength]
With every strength movement, breathe out and never hold your breath. This protects your pelvic floor and your core.

Let's practise it once now, sitting down and with full attention. Breathe in and let everything widen. Breathe out and imagine you are about to lift something heavy, like a full shopping bag. Your pelvic floor lifts, your belly firms, and only then comes the movement. Ten times: in, out and lift.

[Meditation · Progressive muscle relaxation]
Lie on your side and make yourself comfortable with pillows.

We are now going to tense individual parts of the body very lightly, one after the other, and then consciously release them. Begin with your feet: curl your toes a little, hold briefly and let go. Then your hands: make a gentle fist and let go again. Then your shoulders: draw them a little up towards your ears and let them become heavy. Finally your face: squeeze your eyes shut for a moment and let everything soften.

Notice how your body feels now. Heavier, warmer, calmer.

[CLOSING]
Strength is not the opposite of softness. A strong body can relax so much more easily.

[0:00 · ARRIVING]
Lovely to have you here. In this video we move together through the exercises from our session "Strength for everyday life with your baby", so that you can repeat them at home whenever you like and at your own pace. Have a mat, a cushion and a blanket ready, and if anything does not feel good along the way, take a break or simply leave that exercise out.

[Squats · 3 × 10]
Stand hip-width apart, arms in front of you. As you breathe in, sit back and down, as if you were sitting onto a chair. As you breathe out, lift your pelvic floor and press up through your heels.
[To progress: hold your baby or a weight.]

[Reverse lunge · 2 × 8 each side]
Hold on to the back of a chair. Take a big step back with your right leg and lower your knee towards the floor. As you breathe out, come back through your front heel. Then the other side.
[Your front knee stays above your foot.]

[Single-leg glute bridge · 2 × 8 each side]
Lie on your back with your feet on the floor. Stretch one leg out long. As you breathe out, lift your pelvic floor and press up through the heel on the floor. Your pelvis stays level. As you breathe in, lower down.
[Too hard? Start with both feet down.]

[Kneeling side plank · 2 × 20 seconds each side]
Lie on your side, support yourself on your forearm, knees bent. As you breathe out, lift your hips until knees, hips and head form a line. Keep breathing calmly and hold.
[To progress: straighten your legs.]

[Band row · 2 × 12]
Fix the band to a door handle or loop it around your feet. As you breathe out, draw your elbows back and your shoulder blades together. As you breathe in, let them move forward slowly.
[Shoulders stay away from your ears.]

[Breathwork · Breathing under effort]
In every strength exercise: breathe out on the effort, breathe in on the release. Let's practise it standing, with a squat.

Breathe in and sit back and down. Breathe out, lift your pelvic floor and come up. Feel how your whole body connects in this moment. Five repetitions, very consciously with your breath.

[Meditation · I am strong and I am held]
Lie down and let your body become heavy after your workout.

Feel your heart still beating a little faster and slowly becoming calmer. Feel the warmth in your muscles. Your body is strong. It carried a child, gave birth, and now it carries your child every single day.

And at the same time you are allowed to be held, by the floor beneath you, by the people around you. Say to yourself: I am strong, and I am held.

[CLOSING]
You have already become so much stronger. Keep going, with patience and with joy.
map.[Talking head · straight to camera · app:
[Talking head · straight to camera · approx. 7 min.]

Hi, it's lovely to have you back. Our seventh session was about a question almost every woman asks me at some point: when can I start running again or go back to my sport? Here I'd like to explain in more detail what that depends on and how you can make your way back safely.

[short pause]

Maybe you were told at your postnatal check that you're cleared to do everything again. That check is important, but it mainly looks at whether your womb has returned to its normal size and whether any wounds have healed well. Whether your pelvic floor and your midline are ready for running or jumping is usually not something it answers. When you run, every landing puts several times your body weight through you, and your pelvic floor has to absorb that impact thousands of times in a row.

As a guideline, running and jumping usually only make sense from around twelve weeks after the birth. Those twelve weeks are a minimum, and when it's right for you depends on what your body can already do. Some women are well prepared at twelve weeks, others need six months or longer, especially after a difficult birth or a caesarean. Both are completely fine. Breastfeeding plays a role too, because while you're feeding your tissues are often still a little softer, and some women only notice after weaning that their pelvic floor can handle much more again.

[pause]

That's exactly what the load check we did is for. Each exercise in it tests something you'll need later for running. Single-leg balance shows how well you keep your balance and stabilise your pelvis, because when you run you're only ever on one leg. The single-leg sit-to-stand at a chair tests the strength in your legs and glutes and whether your knee stays steady and in line. The single-leg calf raise shows whether your calves have enough endurance, because they absorb a large part of the impact when you run. Finally, brisk marching on the spot and gentle hops are your first step towards impact, and this is where we pay especially close attention to your pelvic floor.

If you managed all the exercises without symptoms, that's a wonderful sign. If you couldn't manage one of them yet, that's valuable information that shows us where to keep building. By symptoms I mainly mean leaking urine, a feeling of pressure or heaviness downwards, pain in your pelvis, your back or your scar, or noticing that you can only manage the exercise by holding your breath.

[calmer tone]

Once you're ready, it's best to make your way back to running in small steps. Many women start by alternating walking and running, for example one minute of running and two minutes of walking, and slowly lengthen the running sections over several weeks. A well-fitting sports bra makes a big difference, especially if you're breastfeeding, and many women find it helps to feed or pump beforehand. In the beginning, run on even ground and on days when you've slept at least reasonably well.

Running with a pram is a challenge of its own, by the way, because you can't swing your arms freely and you often end up leaning forward. Wait until your baby is old enough and the pram is designed for it, and if in doubt, ask your paediatrician. Until then, brisk walking with the pram is great training, and that's why it's your home practice: twenty minutes of brisk walking twice a week, uphill too if you like. It gets your circulation going and prepares your legs and your pelvic floor for more.

If the movement you love is something else, the same principle applies. Whether it's riding, tennis, skiing or lifting heavy weights, think about what that sport demands of your body and build up exactly those abilities step by step. [your detail: how you found your way back to riding or to your favourite movement after a birth] It's a good idea to see a pelvic health physiotherapist if you still have symptoms after the load check, or if you're planning a sport with a lot of impact or heavy weights.

Finally, one thought about the meditation at the end of our session. Longing for the movement you love is a beautiful thing, because it shows that a part of you wants to come back, a part that may not have had much space in recent months. Let that anticipation carry you, and at the same time give your body the time it needs.

[pause, smile]

In the movement video for this session you'll find the whole load check to follow along with, from single-leg balance to gentle hops, followed by a five-minute full-body flow. You can repeat the check in a few weeks and write your results in your workbook, so you can see how they change.

You're on a really good path back to the movement you love. See you next time.
map.[0:00 · ARRIVING · Body scan]\nToday is:
[0:00 · ARRIVING · Body scan]
Today is one of those tired days, and that is completely all right. Lie down on your back, place your feet on the floor, and pull a blanket over you if you like. Today we'll do almost everything lying down. First let your attention travel to your feet and feel where they touch the floor. Then to your legs, to your pelvis and to your belly, rising and falling with every breath. Feel your shoulders, your neck and your face. You don't have to change anything, you're only noticing how you are today. That is exactly what this first week of Unfold is about, an honest look.

[3:00 · RELEASING · Pelvic Tilts · 6 slow rounds]
Stay on your back. As you breathe in, tilt your pelvis very gently forward, so a little tunnel forms under your lower back. As you breathe out, press your lower back carefully into the floor and engage your belly very lightly. And then let everything go and simply rest there for one breath. Notice how it feels to let go after holding, because often that is the only moment we realise how much we have been holding on to all day.

[6:00 · Windshield Wipers · 1 min.]
Place your feet a little wider apart and let both knees sink slowly to the right, then to the left, like windscreen wipers. Your head can roll the other way. Let the movement be heavy and lazy, without any goal at all.

[7:00 · Bridge Pose (Setu Bandhasana) · roll up and down 3 times]
Place your feet hip-width apart again. As you breathe out, roll your pelvis off the floor vertebra by vertebra until you're in a small bridge. As you breathe in, stay up for a moment, and with the next breath out roll slowly back down, vertebra by vertebra, as if you were laying a string of pearls on the floor.

[10:00 · WINDING DOWN · Supine Twist (Supta Matsyendrasana) · 6 breaths each side]
Draw both knees into your chest and then let them sink together to the right towards the floor. Spread your arms out to the sides, and your gaze can go to the left. Breathe into your left side and feel your back lengthen. To come out, bring your knees back to the middle as you breathe in and change sides.

[12:00 · Extended exhale · 6 rounds]
Come back onto your back. Breathe in for four and out for six, without any effort. If you lose count, that's fine, just start again at one.

[13:00 · Savasana · 2 min.]
Now let everything go. Today you took time for yourself even though you're tired, and that is already a lot. If you like, say to yourself silently: I am allowed to be slow. Stay here as long as you like.
map.[0:00 · ARRIVING · Orienting · 1 min.]\n:
[0:00 · ARRIVING · Orienting · 1 min.]
Come to standing and let your gaze wander slowly through the room. This week Unfold is about courage and visibility, about letting yourself be seen for who you are and what you're planning. Becoming visible begins in the body, by taking up space. So today, we take up all the room we want.

[1:00 · Lateral breathing · 5 breaths]
Place your hands on your ribs and breathe wide into your sides.

[3:00 · MOVEMENT · Arm sweeps in all directions · 2 min.]
Reach your arms out in every direction, as far as you can. Up, to the side, back, on the diagonal. Turn along with them, take big steps, take up all the space around you. Maybe it feels unusual at first. Stay with it anyway.

[5:00 · Arm Circles · 1 min.]
Circle your arms big and slow.

[6:00 · Body Roll · 6 waves]
Let a wave run through your whole body.

[10:00 · STRENGTH WITHOUT EXHAUSTION · Side Lunge · 8 each side]
Take big steps to the side and send your hips back. As you breathe out, push back.

[12:30 · Squat · 10]
Feet a little wider than hip-width, and sink deep into the squat.

[14:00 · Forearm Plank · 30 sec.]
Come onto your forearms and hold for thirty seconds.

[15:00 · Modified Side Plank · 20 sec. each side]
Turn onto your side, lift your hips and reach your top arm towards the ceiling. Make yourself wide, from the hand on the floor to the hand in the air.

[18:00 · YOGA FLOW · Goddess Pose with wide arms · 5 breaths]
Feet wide, knees deeply bent, and spread your arms as wide as you can.

[20:00 · Warrior II · 5 breaths each side]
Turn into Warrior II and reach your arms long to both sides. Look over your front hand, forward, into your future.

[22:30 · Triangle (Trikonasana) · 5 breaths each side]
Straighten your front leg, reach your upper body forward and tilt into Triangle. Your top hand points to the ceiling.

[25:00 · WINDING DOWN · Bridge Pose · 3 times]
Lie on your back and roll your pelvis up and down three times.

[27:00 · Savasana with arms spread wide · 2 min.]
Stay lying down and spread your arms wide to the sides, palms up, legs a little further apart. Take up as much space as you like. You are allowed to be seen, with everything you are. Stay here as long as you like.

map.[0:00 · ANKOMMEN]\n\nHallo, und herzlich:
[0:00 · ANKOMMEN]

Hallo, und herzlich willkommen. Kommt rein, kommt rein.

Ich sehe euch nach und nach ankommen und möchte jede von euch richtig begrüßen. {names}. Ich freue mich so, dass ihr da seid.

Bevor wir anfangen, stelle ich mich kurz für alle vor, die neu hier sind. Ich bin Vivien, aber sagt gern einfach Viv zu mir. Ich unterrichte Yoga, Bodyweight-Training und achtsame Bewegung hier in den Tiroler Bergen, ich bin Mama von vier Kindern, und dieser Kreis liegt mir sehr am Herzen.

[optional: noch ein Satz über dich, zum Beispiel warum du diesen Kreis begonnen hast]

Und noch ein kleiner Hinweis für unsere gemeinsame Zeit: Bitte schaltet euer Mikrofon stumm, damit wir einander gut hören. Eure Kamera darf gern an bleiben, sie muss es aber nicht. Ihr dürft sie jederzeit ausschalten, für eure Privatsphäre oder während der Atemübungen, wenn ihr ganz bei euch sein möchtet.

Wenn du gerade noch deinen Platz suchst, lass dir Zeit. Vielleicht steht eine Tasse Tee neben dir, vielleicht hast du gerade ein Kind ins Bett gebracht, vielleicht trägst du noch deine Arbeitskleidung. Wie auch immer du heute angekommen bist, es ist genau richtig. Du musst nicht bereit sein, du musst nur hier sein.

Willkommen bei {title}. In den nächsten fünfzehn Minuten gibt es nichts, was du tun, in Ordnung bringen oder richtig machen musst. Wenn du lieber mit geschlossenen Augen zuhörst, ist auch das völlig in Ordnung.

[Pause]

[1:30 · LANDEN]

Bevor wir sprechen, lasst uns gemeinsam ankommen.

Lass deine Schultern ein kleines bisschen sinken und deinen Kiefer weich werden. Wenn du magst, leg eine Hand auf deine Brust.

Atme langsam durch die Nase ein und lass den Atem zuerst in deinen Bauch fließen und dann in deine Rippen.

Und atme lang und langsam durch den Mund aus, als würdest du eine Fensterscheibe anhauchen.

[gemeinsam atmen]

Noch einmal. Ein durch die Nase … und ein langer, langsamer Atemzug hinaus.

Und ein letztes Mal, und diesmal darf beim Ausatmen ein kleiner Laut mitkommen, wenn du möchtest. Ein Seufzer ist hier ausdrücklich erlaubt.

[hörbar ausatmen]

Schön. Willkommen in deinem Körper. Er hat dich den ganzen Tag getragen.

[3:00 · DAS THEMA HEUTE]

Ich möchte heute über etwas sprechen, das, glaube ich, fast jede Frau in diesem Kreis kennt.

Es ist dieses Gefühl am Ende eines langen Tages, wenn du dich endlich hinsetzt und eine kleine Stimme in dir sagt: Ich habe heute nichts geschafft.

Du warst beschäftigt, seit du aufgewacht bist, und du wurdest den ganzen Tag gebraucht. Und trotzdem fühlt es sich beim Zurückblicken so an, als hättest du nichts vorzuweisen.

Ich kenne dieses Gefühl sehr gut. Und heute möchte ich dir erzählen, warum ich dieser Stimme nicht mehr glaube.

[4:30 · MEINE GESCHICHTE]

Ich bin Mama von vier Kindern. Mein ältestes Kind ist schon ein Teenager, mein jüngstes ist noch nicht einmal zwei, und dazwischen gibt es noch zwei kleine Menschen, die mich auf ganz unterschiedliche Weise brauchen. Wir leben in den Bergen in Tirol, die Eltern meines Mannes wohnen gleich nebenan, und wir helfen mit, einen kleinen Hof zu versorgen.

Meine Tage sind also voll, manchmal so voll, dass ich gar nicht merke, wie sie vergehen.

Und es gibt Abende, an denen ich im Bett liege und im Kopf eine Liste mache von allem, was ich an diesem Tag eigentlich tun wollte. Die E-Mail, die ich nicht beantwortet habe. Das Training, das ich nicht gemacht habe. Das, was ich mir selbst versprochen hatte, nur für mich, und was schon wieder nicht passiert ist.

Und dann spüre ich es: Ich habe heute nichts geschafft.

[Pause]

[dein Detail: ein echter Tag aus den letzten Wochen, zum Beispiel wie der Morgen aussah, wer dich gebraucht hat, was du getragen hast]

Aber eines Abends habe ich etwas anderes ausprobiert. Statt der Liste mit allem, was ich nicht geschafft hatte, habe ich die Liste mit allem gemacht, was ich tatsächlich getan habe.

Ich bin in der Nacht für ein Baby aufgestanden. Ich habe Frühstück für vier Kinder gemacht, die alle etwas anderes wollten. Ich habe den verlorenen Schuh gefunden. Ich habe mir eine Geschichte über eine Freundschaft in der Schule angehört, die wirklich wichtig war. Ich habe jemanden getröstet, der traurig war, und an einen Termin gedacht, an den sonst niemand gedacht hat. Ich habe gearbeitet und gekocht, und ich habe öfter „Ich hab dich lieb“ gesagt, als ich zählen konnte.

Und dann saß ich da und dachte: Das ist nicht nichts. Damit halte ich ein ganzes Leben zusammen.

Das Problem war nie, dass ich zu wenig geschafft habe. Das Problem war, dass niemand diese Art von Arbeit zählt, und deshalb habe ich irgendwann selbst aufgehört, sie zu zählen.

[8:00 · DU BIST DRAN]

Deshalb möchte ich dich einladen, das jetzt gemeinsam mit mir auszuprobieren.

Denk an deinen heutigen Tag. Nicht an das, was du nicht geschafft hast, sondern an das, was du getan hast, auch an die unsichtbaren Dinge. Das, was du getragen hast. Den Menschen, für den du da warst. Den Moment, in dem du weitergemacht hast, obwohl du eigentlich aufhören wolltest.

Und wenn du magst, schreib eines davon in den Chat. Nur eines, und es darf ganz klein sein. „Ich war pünktlich in der Arbeit.“ „Ich habe heute nicht geschimpft.“ „Ich habe meine Mama angerufen.“ Hier zählt alles.

[warten und einige Antworten liebevoll vorlesen, mit Namen, wenn sie nicht anonym sind]

[warm reagieren, zum Beispiel:] Schaut euch das an. Schaut, was dieser Kreis heute alles getragen hat.

Wenn du nichts schreiben möchtest, ist das völlig in Ordnung. Sag es dir einfach leise selbst: Das habe ich heute getan.

[10:00 · EINE KLEINE ÜBUNG]

Lasst uns dieses Gefühl für einen Moment in den Körper bringen.

Richte dich ein wenig auf oder bleib einfach so, wie du bist.
